title_original: The Sounds Around Us / Os sons ao redor

blocks.text: Through image and sound, Ítalo Almeida constructs a narrative that recovers forgotten histories of colonial Brazil in his first solo exhibition.
Deri Andrade

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Boca . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: From the Mirante do Observatório, perched high on one of Ouro Preto’s hills at the foot of the Church of Nossa Senhora das Mercês e Misericórdia, the city in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais reveals itself to me in all its grandeur. Looking out across the horizon, I found myself imagining how the memory of this city has been constructed through its architecture, art, landscapes, people, histories of slavery and the sounds I could hear from that elevated vantage point.

Looking into the distance, it is possible to appreciate something of this city’s geography, inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1980, making it the first Brazilian site to receive this recognition. From here, one can also hear the conversations of residents and the countless tourists who wander its streets each day; the noise of cars travelling over its protected historic roads; the sounds of daily work; students’ laughter; birds in flight; the wind; and the city itself.

These sometimes cacophonous sounds echo Vila Rica’s centuries-old history, the region’s first official name. Historical records place its foundation towards the end of the seventeenth century, around 1698, when the enslavement of Black people was still practised in Brazil, a system officially abolished only on 13 May 1888. During this period, the city, then the capital of Minas Gerais, was a major centre of Brazil’s gold economy.

Mining activity began to decline between the 1760s and 1770s, reflecting the growing difficulty of extracting gold because of natural and geographical conditions. Political developments, including the Inconfidência Mineira independence conspiracy of 1789 and the transfer of the state capital to Belo Horizonte in 1897, also shaped the city’s circumstances.

Visitors to Ouro Preto can encounter aspects of this history through local tourist guides or by entering one of the many preserved gold mines, with their claustrophobic, eerily silent tunnels and underground galleries. Here, the absence of sound exposes a form of tourism that continues to revisit traumatic and violent histories. Those whose livelihoods and identities are connected to them often recount these histories with pride. Rarely subjected to critical examination, romanticised accounts often colour these visits, passed down through local oral traditions. Nevertheless, historians, guides, and storytellers who seek to reveal other dimensions of these narratives deserve recognition, drawing on significant testimonies preserved both orally and in written historical records.

Some of these histories profoundly affected the artist Ítalo Almeida (b. 1996, São Paulo). After spending time in Ouro Preto and subsequently living there for four months from December 2024, as part of an artistic residency organised by the Museu da Inconfidência, Almeida became not only a resident but, above all, a listener to the city’s stories.

The mountainous landscape visible from his window, a geography shaped by both extraordinary beauty and histories of oppression, captivated Almeida, just as it had attracted me during one of my visits to the city. Yet the artist was not entirely seduced by the dark, narrow streets of the former Vila Rica. He told me that the experience could also be difficult. Italo Almeida, Gunga . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Gunga . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: For an artist whose practice has largely centred on images — Almeida is particularly recognised for his photographic work — learning to pay attention to the surrounding sounds became a daily exercise.

“For a city man, walking through the streets of Cabeças in the early hours of the morning was terribly quiet. It was one of the neighbourhoods where I lived during that period. It seemed easier to hear the wind moving through the mist than the sound of other human beings. And then everything would begin again at 4.50 in the morning,” he writes in his account of the experience.
Here, what might ordinarily have been perceived as an image becomes an awareness of sound.

Beyond his daily routine, Almeida gained access to several local archives that stimulated his interest in researching the musical histories of Ouro Preto. Particularly significant was the collection assembled by Francisco Curt Lange, the renowned German-Uruguayan musicologist responsible for some of the most important research into South American musical traditions. Part of this archive originated from religious brotherhoods, notably the Black Brotherhoods of Our Lady of the Rosary. Immersing himself in Curt Lange’s collection, the artist made several discoveries.

Unlike the visible contributions of Black artisans to the city’s Baroque architecture, particularly its churches, Black contributions to music were enveloped in European musical notation and conventions. In local churches, Black craftsmanship survives as evidence of resistance, revealing, for example, the period’s religious syncretism through Adinkra symbols incorporated into church altars. One might recall Antônio Francisco Lisboa, known as Aleijadinho (c. 1738–1814), one of Brazil’s greatest sculptors, whose works can be found throughout the region.

Through his research, Almeida established that “African or Indigenous elements are absent from the majority of these Black musical compositions, which were created under the absolute surveillance of the Catholic Church”. He emphasises that this helps explain why such compositions followed European musical models.
Beyond these official compositions, however, another form of sound attracted Almeida’s attention.

Ouro Preto is also recognised for producing aluminium and related materials. Research identifies the city as one of the places where Brazil’s aluminium industry began, largely because of bauxite deposits. According to various studies, the establishment of Elquisa (Eletro Química Brasileira S/A) led to the production of the country’s first primary aluminium ingot in the Saramenha district during the mid-1930s. Producing this metal also introduced industrial noise into the lives of factory workers and surrounding communities. Italo Almeida, Cavaleiros . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Cavaleiros . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: These sounds became part of Almeida’s research during the residency. He was also interested in the relationship between the local community, including workers at the aluminium factory that remains in operation, and the Black musical traditions associated with the region’s Congado Mineiro groups.

All these elements, the artist recalls, formed the foundation of his first solo exhibition, Ruídos se Organizam (Noises Organise Themselves), presented at the Museu da Inconfidência between August and November 2026.

Through his engagement with the museum’s displayed collections and storage facilities, Almeida expressed indignation at the limited prominence given to Indigenous and Black cultures, and to the historical contributions of individuals from these communities, within the institution’s permanent exhibitions.

By contrast, Joaquim José da Silva Xavier, known as Tiradentes, a leading figure in the Inconfidência Mineira movement, occupies a prominent position in the museum’s displays and gallery signage. Meanwhile, the domestic lives of the white population of European descent are extensively represented through preserved furniture, silverware, personal possessions, clothing and other objects, as the artist himself observes.

Nevertheless, the Museu da Inconfidência’s importance to Brazil and its history is indisputable. Inaugurated on 11 August 1944, the museum occupies the former Town Hall and Prison of Vila Rica. Its imposing building, situated in Praça Tiradentes, exemplifies late-Baroque colonial architecture designed in the 1780s. The institution also encompasses four auxiliary buildings.

As the museum itself explains, “the transformation of the building into a museum formed part of a broader movement driven by Vargas’s Estado Novo and Brazilian modernism during the first half of the twentieth century.”

It is equally important to acknowledge the work of museum director Alex Calheiros and curator Ana Avelar, who have developed a dynamic programme attuned to contemporary concerns. The museum currently receives an average of 350,000 visitors annually, making it one of the most visited institutions in Minas Gerais. Italo Almeida, Boca . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Boca . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: Recent interventions in its exhibition programme have included presentations by the Instituto de Arte Contemporânea de Ouro Preto and artists such as João Trevisan, whose series of abstract paintings entered into dialogue with the museum’s existing collection.

Confronted with these other histories, Ítalo Almeida conceived an exhibition curated by Ana Avelar that responds directly to his experience of living in Ouro Preto, listening to its stories and sounds, and immersing himself in archival research.

Six works occupy the museum’s galleries, bringing to the surface what has remained hidden or silenced. The newly created Miserere No. 1, JANTAR, Gunga I, Confia na Boca and Cavaleiros I and II translate the months of artistic residency into new forms of experimentation within Almeida’s practice.
Working with aluminium and soapstone, another abundant material in the region, the artist created the installation Miserere No. 1.

The work consists of four aluminium towers equipped with loudspeakers, reinterpreting the composition of the same name by Manoel Dias de Oliveira, one of the Black musicians represented in Curt Lange’s archive.

“Each tower emits a different frequency range, and the towers and their speakers are interconnected by elastic bands that reproduce the compressions of musical frequencies. These compressions move the elastic bands in different directions, allowing us not only to hear but also to visualise the sonic conflict between the towers.”
Almeida explains that his decision to construct four towers refers to the statues positioned above the museum, flanking the building as though protecting it.

Unlike the punitive symbolism associated with these sculptures — one of which represents Justice — the installation incorporates Adinkra symbols carved from soapstone by artisans from Santa Rita de Ouro Preto.
These are the same symbols encountered in the artworks and architectural details of Ouro Preto’s churches, constructed by Black people during the colonial period.

Through this intervention, the artist restores dignity to the musicians and artists of the slaveholding colonial era, “men who sought a place in society and who used music as a profession through which to achieve social mobility”. Italo Almeida, Miserere . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Miserere . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: It is no coincidence that the installation occupies one of the building’s most imposing rooms, where the flag of Minas Gerais appears to look down on it.

By placing these threads, and consequently these histories, under tension, the artist orchestrates the recovery of figures rarely mentioned in historical literature and largely unknown to the wider public.
Among them are the trumpeters.
Drawing on texts by Lucas Figueiredo, the photographs Cavaleiros I and II turn their attention to these nineteenth-century figures.
In Almeida’s photographs, however, young horse riders from the more peripheral neighbourhoods of Ouro Preto play the trumpets, where the artist lived for part of his residency.

These young men are often seen riding through the city on horseback. Often travelling in groups, with portable speakers playing contemporary popular music, the riders are a familiar presence at local events and in everyday life.
Historically, trumpeters announced the arrival of people from the hills surrounding the city. Today, peripheral neighbourhoods occupy parts of this same geography.

In these locations, including Parque das Andorinhas and Morro da Queimada, Almeida chose to produce his photographs using the visual narrative technique of tableau vivant, a recurring feature of his practice.

For the two horse riders, the artist dressed one young man in period clothing, constructing an image of a historical figure for whom no visual record exists. The other rider wears his own clothes, situating the photograph firmly in the present and re-enacting the scene in a documentary style that evokes everyday life. Italo Almeida, Gunga . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida, Gunga . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: Another sonic element that inspired the works exhibited at the museum was gossip and the act of producing sound through conversation.
In Confia na Boca (Trust the Mouth), oral tradition becomes a tribute to a fundamental pillar of Black culture in Brazil.
Through speech, Almeida constructs a technologically mediated work incorporating video and sound.

During his residency, he recorded conversations, personal accounts, anecdotes, gossip and storytelling, filling his mobile phone with the voices and memories of the city. He recognised in this accumulation of confidences the possibility of creating a new artwork.

Within the imposing architecture of a building that once functioned as a prison, complete with cells, Confia na Boca evokes a “Tower of Babel”, in which the architectural elements of walls are replaced aesthetically by recordings displayed on small screens.
The technical devices employed by the artist reveal a particular concern with audience interaction, since the work deactivates when the room becomes crowded and noisy.

“Like all gossip, it cannot be shared with a large number of people. A microphone in the work measures the decibel levels produced by museum visitors. If there are too many visitors, the work displays another image and ‘stops confessing’, allowing for a different form of interaction.”
Elsewhere in the museum, visitors encounter Gunga I, which reflects Almeida’s engagement with the region’s Congado Mineiro traditions.

“Gunga” is the name given to a musical instrument used in this Brazilian cultural practice. Participants wear the instrument attached to their feet and ankles while dancing, producing sounds through small objects fastened to leather or fabric straps, including rattles, jingles and small metal bells.
In Almeida’s installation, the instrument is stylised. Italo Ameida, Jantar . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Ameida, Jantar . Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: Made from aluminium, the work was conceived through the relationship between participants in Congado and Reisado traditions and their employment in the metallurgical industry.

Here, relationships that alternately converge and diverge are translated into an industrial logic. As the artist explains, he chose to develop a kinetic sculpture whose operation depends on physical forces, just as the sounds produced by the musicians’ feet do.
It is particularly interesting to observe how sound is understood throughout the exhibition as a material that occupies space.
In JANTAR (Dinner), for example, the intersection between the artist’s work and the museum’s collection becomes even more apparent.
Using an object from the Museu da Inconfidência’s collection, Almeida deliberately places an element of his installation on a table in the gallery devoted to antique furniture.
The small aluminium object stands out against the wooden furniture because of its contrasting materiality. Yet another element invites visitors to approach it.

A sound device emits conversations, the noises of food preparation and the clinking of cutlery during dinner in two households situated on the same street, only a few metres apart, yet belonging to different neighbourhoods.
One family lives in Vila dos Engenheiros, while the other resides in Vila dos Operários.

“Separated by only one main street, the two neighbourhoods operate at opposing frequencies. […] The point at which these lives converge is the ‘white elephant’ that created them: the aluminium factory. Now obsolete, the industry that once promised progress instead delivers pollution and residential immobility.”
In his first solo exhibition, Ruídos se Organizam , Ítalo Almeida captures the essence of Ouro Preto through listening and sound. Italo Almeida. Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.caption: Italo Almeida. Image courtesy of Yuji Kodato.

blocks.text: The depth of his research during the months he spent among its residents, engaging with the routines and noises of a city that resists the passage of time while opening itself to the present, provides an essential foundation for the future development of his practice.
Following the artist’s trajectory, and the choices he has orchestrated over the years, is therefore a rewarding experience when considered within the genealogy of his work.

A photographer and filmmaker by vocation, whose productions have already appeared in exhibitions and film festivals around the world, Almeida is pursuing a path that deserves to be followed, seen, and heard.

The multimedia installations presented at the Museu da Inconfidência reinforce the histories that have emerged from this place — histories spoken, whispered, gossiped about, sung, proclaimed and preserved.

If the surrounding sounds of this historic city have managed to penetrate the museum’s walls and imposing doors, their echoes will continue to reverberate, leaving a resounding imprint on the history told and the everyday life of this place.

Deri Andrade is a Brazilian researcher, journalist and curator at Instituto Inhotim in Brumadinho, Brazil. His research and curatorial practice focus on Afro-Brazilian artistic production, cultural heritage and the visibility of Black artists within contemporary art histories and institutional collections. He co-founded Projeto Afro, a research and mapping platform that documents and disseminates the work of Afro-Brazilian artists. At Inhotim, Andrade has curated and co-curated several exhibitions, including Direito à Forma and Davi de Jesus do Nascimento’s solo exhibition, Tororama . His work helps expand critical discourse around Black artistic practices and their representation within Brazil’s cultural institutions.
